title: The Latte Line on trial
intro: The Latte Line started as a joke and ended up on Wikipedia. Here is what people say about it, checked against the data. Each test compares real Sydney with random Sydneys that are just as smooth.
footer: Sources of the claims: the Wikipedia article 'Latte Line' and the press it cites. Tests: experiments/latte_claims.py (results/latte_claims/claims.csv). The lockdown councils use the exact NSW council boundaries (Geoscape, data.gov.au). Of the six claims with a p-value, only the lockdown one survives a correction for testing all six. We never test heritage or ethnicity against a line.

items.claim: It splits north-east from south-west Sydney, from the airport through Parramatta
items.finding: 77% of suburbs sit on the side that description predicts, against 50% for random Sydneys (p = 0.03). After allowing for the six claims we tested with a p-value, p = 0.08: likely, but not proven.

items.claim: It's a figure of speech, not something in the coffee data
items.finding: Count cafés against fast-food places and Sydney really does sort into a café north-east and a fast-food south-west (p = 0.002). The border is cleaner than random on its own (p = 0.02), but not once we allow for the six food lines we tried (p = 0.12): a slope more than a wall.

items.claim: There's a Latte Line in other cities too
items.verdict: Partly holds, and it's the line that travels furthest
items.finding: Cafés and fast food sort apart in all 29 cities we tested. Pooled over the 11 cities we held back, the line is real (p = 0.02, after checking the pooling against maps with no line and allowing for every line we pooled). We found this by pooling every line, not as a written prediction, so our European cities are the real test: it held in southern Europe (Barcelona, Paris, Marseille, Rome) but not in the Netherlands, Sweden or Denmark. It passes outright in Brisbane, Fukuoka, Los Angeles and San Francisco.

items.claim: The Red Rooster Line marks where Red Rooster restaurants stop
items.finding: Whether a Red Rooster or a Messina gelato shop is nearer splits Sydney more cleanly than chance on its own (p = 0.03), but not after allowing for the six food lines we tried (p = 0.16).

items.claim: It divides the haves from the have-nots
items.verdict: Same direction, but money is a slope
items.finding: Rent, mortgage and household income all fall the same way, but none forms a line (p = 0.14 to 0.22). Money follows the jobs divide (75 to 79% of suburbs) more closely than the café one (66 to 72%).

items.claim: Homes above the line are worth over $1m, below it under
items.finding: Sale prices aren't in the Census. By mortgage repayments, 70% of café-side suburbs are above Sydney's median and 79% of fast-food-side suburbs below.

items.claim: Which side you live on shapes how you do at school
items.finding: School results aren't in the Census, but university degrees are: 77% of suburbs fall on the matching side, against 50% for random Sydneys (p = 0.01; 0.07 after allowing for the six claims we tested with a p-value).

items.claim: The 2021 lockdown's 'councils of concern' were the line's other side
items.finding: 78% of their residents lived on the fast-food side. The lockdown map matched the Latte Line far better than random Sydneys do (80% vs 50%, p = 0.005; 0.03 after allowing for the six claims we tested with a p-value), and the jobs line slightly better still (82%). This shows where the rules fell, not whether they were fair.

items.verdict: Not in the Census up to 2021
items.finding: The jobs line was a real line in every Census from 2001 to 2021, about equally sharp each time. The 2023 claim is about poverty since 2021, which the next Census can test.

items.claim: It's breaking down as western chicken chains spread east
items.finding: Whether an El Jannah or a Starbucks is nearer no longer splits Sydney (could be chance, p = 0.85). We have no older shop maps to show it once did.

items.claim: Melbourne's divide is much weaker than Sydney's
items.finding: Under the same test Sydney has two real lines (the Hi-Vis and Factory Lines) and Melbourne none.

items.claim: The west is hotter, with less shade and tree cover
items.finding: Heat and tree canopy aren't in our data.

items.claim: It's an 'ethnic' west against an affluent north-east
items.finding: We never score heritage against a line. The Heritage tab shows where people born overseas live, side by side, and leaves it there.
